---
title: Connectors
description: How a connector brings records from another service into Marfa, and what the instance keeps so it can stop and resume safely.
---

Much of what a person keeps starts somewhere else: events in Google Calendar, issues on GitHub, highlights in Readwise. A **connector** is a program outside the server that **registers with the instance**, most often to read such a service, its vendor, and write what it finds as items. It can also carry changes made in Marfa back to the vendor.

The registration is what makes a program a connector. An app or a script that reads and writes with a key, or through a sign-in, but never registers isn't one, and needs nothing on this page.

A Todoist connector, for example, runs where you choose, and Todoist can post webhooks to the instance:

<ConnectorParts />

## A program you run

The server never runs a connector or calls a vendor. A connector is an ordinary program you run wherever suits you, on a schedule or all the time, and it uses the same API as any app. That keeps the server small, and your vendor credentials out of it.

Most connectors are built on **the connector kit**, `@withmarfa/connector`, a TypeScript library in [withmarfa/plugins](https://github.com/withmarfa/plugins). It registers the connector, writes only what changed and reports each run, so your code only talks to the vendor.

## What every connector shares

- **A key of its own.** A connector registers under a key made for it alone, and a key holds one registration; an app's sign-in can't register one. The key holds exactly what the connector writes, write on its types and edge types, which the kit checks on start. You make it from the CLI, as [Build a connector](/build/connector#make-its-key-and-run-it) shows, or, for a plugin's connector, its [connector host](#a-connector-in-a-plugin) gets it from Marfa.
- **A source.** The key's [source](/build/items-and-types#where-an-item-came-from) labels everything the connector writes. It names the system the records come from, such as `github`, never an account. With each record's `source_id`, its ID at the vendor, it lets a connector update a record rather than duplicate it. An account goes into `source_id` only for what it owns, such as a calendar.
- **A name and a mark**, so an app shows "GitHub" with its logo rather than the code. A connector sets only what the source lacks, so a name the owner chose stays, as [Name the source](/build/connector-pull#name-the-source) shows.
- **The feed.** What a connector brings in belongs in the [feed](/build/items-and-types#library-and-feed). It names `feed` on each write, or its key makes `feed` its default; otherwise its records land in the library. A plugin's connector that names no tier writes each kind where its owner's mapping says, and in the feed by default, whatever its key's default tier.
- **Links that mean something.** It links records with the [edge type](/build/edges#edge-types) that fits: a GitHub comment `comments-on` its issue, a Readwise highlight is an `excerpt-of` its book. An edge type it stops writing is **retired**: the kit removes the edges of that type it wrote itself, never one a person drew, so the key keeps write on it.
- **Nothing kept on its own computer.** What it resumes from [lives on the instance](#what-the-instance-keeps-for-a-connector), so it can stop, restart or move without losing its place.
- **One process at a time.** A hold lets one copy write, so two started by mistake don't overwrite each other.

## Edits a connector puts back

A connector that takes no edits back for a type, such as an RSS entry, puts back any edit a person makes there on its next run. **It says so in its registration**, and the type's items read `read_only: true`, so an app can show them locked. Marfa refuses no write for it. [Pull from a vendor](/build/connector-pull#declare-the-types-you-dont-carry-back) shows how.

## What the instance keeps for a connector

The instance keeps what a connector needs to resume:

| What | What it's for |
| --- | --- |
| A registration | Names the connector and the types it holds read only, and shows its last heartbeat and how its recent runs went. |
| A state document | A JSON object the connector resumes from, such as the vendor's sync token. |
| Current problems | Messages about unresolved trouble, such as a record the vendor refused, until the connector clears them. |
| Agreements | One record per item of what the connector and the vendor last agreed about it, so a two-way connector can tell a change a person made from its own. |
| A hold | Lets one process at a time write, so two copies started by mistake don't overwrite each other. |

The state document, current problems and agreements belong to the key's **source**, not to one key. Replace a connector's key with one under the same source, and the connector picks up where it stopped.

## Webhooks from the vendor

A vendor's webhooks let a connector act on a change at once. The instance can give a connector an **inbound endpoint**, a private address the vendor posts to.

The instance stores each delivery as it arrived, and **the connector does the rest**: it reads the deliveries, checks each came from the vendor, and marks them handled. [Receive vendor webhooks](/build/connector-webhooks) shows how.

## A connector in a plugin

A [plugin](/use/install-a-plugin) can bring a connector with its types, and then **Marfa holds what you would otherwise set up by hand:**

- **A connector host** runs it: a program on a machine you link once, which gets the connector's key from Marfa ([Run a plugin's connector](/use/run-a-plugin-connector)).
- **Its settings and secrets** stay in Marfa, and the connector reads them at the start of each run ([Give a connector its settings](/use/connector-settings)).
- **A mapping** chooses the type and tier each kind of record lands as ([Choose where a connector's records land](/use/map-a-connector)).

The connectors in withmarfa/plugins are working examples. Install one as [Install a plugin](/use/install-a-plugin) shows, and [Build a connector](/build/connector) walks through one from the kit's template.

The rules behind this page are in the [connectors](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/connectors.md) and [inbound webhooks](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/inbound-webhooks.md) chapters of the contract, and plugin connectors in the [plugins](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/plugins.md#connector-hosts) chapter.
